name: Microabrasion

lead: Microabrasion clears white or brown spots on the front teeth, including fluorosis marks, so the smile looks more even in colour. The change is visible right after the dentist polishes the tooth.

A mild acid and pumice take off a very thin layer of surface enamel, a few tenths of a millimetre, and the stain goes with it. The method dates to a 1986 technique by Croll and Cavanaugh, and recent clinical trials compare it with resin infiltration and other minimally invasive options.

paras: A dentist applies the acidic abrasive paste to the affected teeth in a single visit, rinses and polishes, and often finishes with a fluoride or protective step. People use it for mild to moderate fluorosis, enamel defects and white spots left after braces, sometimes alongside whitening afterward.

Enamel that is removed does not grow back, and over-thinning can let darker dentine show through. It does not reach stains that sit deep in dentine, such as tetracycline staining. It is carried out by a dentist, and anyone with already thin enamel is a poorer fit.

angle.text: Microabrasion clears white or brown spots, including fluorosis marks, so front teeth look more even in colour. A dentist removes a thin layer of stained enamel, and the surface change shows right after polishing. The method has been in clinical use since the 1980s.

lead: Enamel microabrasion is a cosmetic dental procedure that removes a very thin outer layer of enamel, using a mildly acidic abrasive compound, to reduce surface discolouration such as white or brown spots.[1] The first practical method, using weak hydrochloric acid and pumice, was developed by Theodore Croll and Richard Cavanaugh in 1986.[1]

It is used mainly for dental fluorosis and for enamel defects including white spot lesions after orthodontic appliances.[1][2] It is not suited to discolouration located in dentine, such as tetracycline staining.[1]
Several recent clinical trials, registered mostly from 2019 onward, compare microabrasion with resin infiltration and other minimally invasive options.[3][4]
infobox: A few tenths of a millimetre

paras: The procedure combines mechanical and chemical action to remove superficial enamel. A rubber dam is typically used, which can be hard to place on teeth that have not fully erupted.[1] Before it, stained teeth were often covered with restorations such as porcelain veneers.[1]

A general encyclopedia article says microabrasion should be considered first for mild and moderate fluorosis.[1] It is also used for orthodontic-related defects and developmental enamel defects.[1] Reviews of white spot lesions after orthodontic treatment discuss it among management options.[2]
Thinning enamel can expose dentine, which may look yellowish or darker, and bleaching can be combined to mask this.[1]

A review article gives an overview of clinical and scientific considerations of enamel microabrasion.[3] Registered trials include a completed 60-patient comparison of hydrochloric acid-pumice and sodium hypochlorite-pumice for fluorosis,[4] a split-mouth comparison of resin infiltration and microabrasion for early lesions,[5] and a trial of resin infiltration versus microabrasion with CPP-ACP for fluorotic white spots.[6] Another registered trial compares resin infiltration with a combined microabrasion approach for molar incisor hypomineralisation.[7] Results are not summarised here because outcome data were not available in the sources.

timeline.event: Removal of outermost enamel is first proposed.[1]
